strengths: The paper explores a timely and relatively original direction: treating 2D Gaussian splats as native inputs for vision-language alignment rather than merely compressing RGB-derived tokens after encoding.

The proposed engineering pipeline appears practically useful. Batched CUDA processing reaches high reported GPU utilization and up to 90.3× throughput improvement over the cited implementation, potentially enabling millions of images to be fitted.

Reusing a largely frozen RGB-pretrained CLIP backbone is a sensible parameter-efficient design. Achieving 13–15% ImageNet-1K zero-shot top-1 accuracy while training about 7% of the parameters provides credible initial evidence that splat representations retain semantic information.

The manuscript honestly reports the performance gap to its 18.5% RGB baseline, includes experiments across 400–3136 splats and 98/196 output tokens, and shows that direct training from scratch is substantially less effective.
The paper is generally understandable, and its systems and modeling contributions are organized around a coherent research question.
weaknesses: The central transmission-efficiency claim is not adequately supported. Compression is measured against uncompressed 8-bit RGB arrays, although the motivating edge–cloud setting normally transmits JPEG, AVIF, or another codec. No comparison at matched byte rate or reconstruction quality is provided, and headers, entropy coding, quantization, and serialization costs are omitted. The reported 3–23.5× ratios therefore do not establish an advantage over realistic image transmission.

The claimed computational benefit for multimodal processing is also unverified. The method consumes 400–3136 splats, adds a Perceiver resampler, and still emits 98 or 196 tokens; it reports no end-to-end latency, FLOPs, memory, energy, or attention cost against the RGB pipeline. Thus, the results do not demonstrate relief of the stated token-explosion problem.

The vision-language evaluation is too narrow to substantiate general alignment or transfer claims: it contains only ImageNet-1K zero-shot classification. There are no image–text retrieval results, broader zero-shot classification suites, robustness tests, captioning/VQA tasks, or direct edge–cloud measurements.

Important controls and ablations are missing. The paper does not isolate information loss from splat fitting by rendering the splats and evaluating the RGB encoder, compare against JPEG or downsampled RGB at matched storage, or quantify the effects of structured initialization, luminance pruning, Fourier encoding, covariance scaling, gating, the resampler, and partial backbone unfreezing on downstream accuracy.

The speed evidence is incomplete: only relative speedups are shown, with no absolute fitting throughput or latency, detailed hardware/kernel settings, quality-matched comparison, or accounting for the offline cost of producing the splats. The largest number is obtained at batch size 4096, so it does not establish low-latency edge encoding.

Luminance-based pruning is motivated by the unsupported assumption that dark regions carry little semantic information. Dark objects, text, and low-light content can be crucial, and only qualitative reconstructions—not downstream accuracy or diverse quantitative reconstruction metrics—are presented to validate the pruning rule.

Experimental rigor is limited. Results are shown mainly as a few plotted points without exact tables, repeated runs, error bars, statistical uncertainty, or validation on another dataset. Selecting the RGB checkpoint using ImageNet-1K validation accuracy also makes the same validation set an optimization target rather than a clean final evaluation.

Reproducibility is insufficient for the reported contribution: the manuscript says code will be released later and omits essential details such as the exact DataComp subset construction, fitting loss and optimizer, pruning thresholds and schedule, Fourier frequencies, module dimensions, normalization statistics, and checkpoint-selection procedure for the GS models.

Some quantitative motivation is inaccurate: an energy intensity of 0.1–0.2 kWh/GB implies well below one kWh for a few gigabytes, not “tens of kilowatt-hours.” This is a correctable presentation issue, but it weakens confidence in the edge-energy argument.

Overall, the idea and initial feasibility result are worthwhile, but the main efficiency claims are evaluated against an unrealistic storage baseline and the empirical study is too preliminary to support the paper’s broad conclusions. These material evidence gaps currently outweigh the novelty, leading to a weak reject.

The engineering results are potentially valuable. The reported batched implementation gives 33.5–90.3× speedups across the tested batch sizes, and structured initialization substantially improves the shown reconstruction PSNR at fixed iteration budgets.

The adaptation strategy is computationally economical at training time: it reuses an RGB-pretrained backbone, trains roughly 7% of the parameters, and examines both 98- and 196-token outputs over 400–3,136 splats.

The authors report the performance gap to RGB rather than presenting the method as state of the art, and they acknowledge that codec-side quantization and end-to-end edge–cloud evaluation remain absent.
weaknesses: The central vision-language claim is supported only by zero-shot ImageNet-1K classification. There is no image–text retrieval, compositional evaluation, captioning, VQA, or actual VLM experiment. Thus the evidence establishes limited class-label transfer, not broad vision-language alignment or usefulness as a multimodal substrate.

The comparison set is inadequate. The paper does not compare against JPEG/WebP/AVIF or a learned codec at matched transmitted size, rendered 2DGS images passed through the RGB encoder, prior Gaussian representations, or token-reduction baselines. Consequently, it does not isolate whether the proposed representation is preferable to much simpler compression or adaptation alternatives.

The claimed 3–23.5× compression is measured against an uncompressed pixel array while the motivating deployment already transmits formats such as JPEG. The splats remain float16 and no serialized or entropy-coded sizes are reported. Encoding/fitting cost, transfer latency, decoding cost, and end-to-end energy are also unmeasured, so the practical transmission-efficiency claim is not substantiated.

The checkpoint is selected using the highest zero-shot accuracy on the ImageNet-1K validation set and then evaluated on that same set. This model-selection leakage makes the reported result optimistically biased. The absence of multiple seeds, uncertainty estimates, and a separate selection set further weakens small comparisons such as 98 versus 196 tokens.

The token-efficiency motivation is not demonstrated. The model consumes 400–3,136 splats before resampling, while its better configuration emits the same 196 tokens as the RGB baseline. No FLOPs, memory, attention cost, throughput, or downstream context-length measurements are provided; the only token-reduced 98-token variant performs worse.

The systems contribution lacks sufficient benchmarking detail. Only relative speedup and utilization are given, without absolute fitting throughput or latency, memory consumption, hardware and kernel settings for the fitting benchmark, numerical-equivalence checks, or a complete comparison protocol. A statement that code will be released later does not provide present reproducibility.

Structured initialization and pruning are evaluated mainly through isolated visual examples. The initialization PSNR values appear to come from a single image, with no dataset averages or variability. Pruning has no quantitative rate–distortion or downstream-semantic ablation, and the assumption that low luminance indicates low semantic information is unjustified and can fail for dark objects or scenes.

There are no component ablations for Fourier features, covariance log scaling, gating, normalization, global mean pooling, the Perceiver resampler, or the number of unfrozen layers. Hence it is unclear which proposed elements matter or whether a simpler set encoder would perform similarly.

Reproducibility is poor: the exact DataComp subset and sampling procedure, fitting losses and iteration schedules, pruning hyperparameters, Fourier frequencies, stem dimensions, resampler depth, and several normalization details are missing. The manuscript also contains inconsistencies such as 3–20× versus 3–23.5× compression, a claimed 3–5 point gap despite a worst displayed gap of about 5.7 points, six adaptation epochs versus 30-epoch plots, and mismatched or duplicated Figure 7 plot labels.

Overall, the problem and engineering direction have merit, but the current evidence is preliminary and does not support the paper’s principal efficiency and multimodal-alignment claims. These are material experimental and methodological gaps rather than presentation-only refinements, so the balance favors weak rejection.

The proposed pipeline is practically motivated and coherent: structured initialization and batched fitting enable dataset-scale preparation, while the splat-aware stem and Perceiver Resampler provide a reasonable mechanism for connecting variable-size Gaussian sets to a pretrained ViT.

Experiments are conducted at meaningful scale on 12.8M DataComp image-text pairs. The adapted models retain nontrivial zero-shot ImageNet performance—approximately 13–15% top-1 versus 18.5% for the paper’s RGB model—while training only about 7% of the parameters.

The reported accuracy is fairly stable from 3136 to 900 splats, corresponding to roughly 3–12× compression under the paper’s raw-storage calculation. This is useful preliminary evidence that Gaussian representations preserve some semantic signal beyond reconstruction fidelity.

The manuscript is generally understandable, motivates the systems and modeling components clearly, and acknowledges important limitations such as the remaining RGB accuracy gap and omission of codec-side quantization.
weaknesses: The central efficiency case is not adequately demonstrated. Compression is measured against uncompressed pixel storage using float16 splat parameters, whereas the motivating edge–cloud setting normally transmits JPEG or another coded bitstream. There is no comparison against JPEG or modern codecs at matched byte rate and accuracy, and no end-to-end measurements of encoding cost, transmitted bytes, energy, latency, memory, or throughput. Consequently, the claimed practical transmission advantage remains speculative.

The method does not convincingly address the stated token-explosion problem. The main configuration resamples the splats to 196 tokens—the same count as the RGB ViT baseline—and the reduced configuration still uses 98 tokens. Moreover, the Perceiver must attend over as many as 3136 input splats. Encoder FLOPs, Perceiver overhead, memory, and latency are not reported, so compact storage cannot be assumed to imply cheaper model execution.

Evidence for vision-language alignment is too narrow for the breadth of the claims. Evaluation consists only of zero-shot ImageNet classification; there is no image–text retrieval, compositional or fine-grained evaluation, additional classification datasets, or downstream multimodal task. Thus it is unclear whether the representation preserves broadly aligned semantic information rather than enough information for this single benchmark.

Several claimed technical contributions receive insufficient controlled evaluation. The 90.3× result compares a highly batched implementation at batch size 4096 against an unbatched prior implementation, but absolute throughput, fitting time, hardware-matched baselines, reconstruction quality at matched compute, and a breakdown of batching versus kernel improvements are absent. Likewise, structured initialization is supported mainly by one visual example and isolated PSNR values, while pruning is illustrated using one image without dataset-level rate–distortion or downstream-accuracy results.

The luminance-pruning rationale is technically questionable: dark regions are not necessarily low-information or semantically unimportant. No experiment tests failure cases involving dark objects, night scenes, or demographic/appearance variation, and no ablation separates the effects of L1 regularization and luminance thresholding. Therefore the claim that pruning preserves semantically important content is unsupported.

The RGB and GS training protocols are not directly comparable despite the claim of identical conditions: the RGB model is trained for 32 epochs, whereas GS adaptation runs for six epochs with most of the pretrained model frozen. This setup demonstrates transfer feasibility but does not isolate whether performance differences arise from the input representation, optimization duration, trainable capacity, or architecture. Selecting checkpoints using ImageNet-1K validation accuracy and reporting performance on that same validation set also introduces benchmark-specific model-selection bias.

Reproducibility is presently weak. The code is only promised for future release, and the paper omits exact DataComp subset construction, splat-fitting iteration settings for the training corpus, pruning hyperparameters, architecture dimensions, Fourier frequencies, Perceiver depth and attention configuration, preprocessing details, and sufficient CUDA benchmarking methodology. Results also lack multiple seeds or uncertainty estimates.

Presentation issues—including inconsistent claims of a 3–5 point versus roughly 3.5–5.5 point top-1 gap, a likely ViT width typo of 716 rather than 768, and calling fixed-iteration results “asymptotic” quality—are readily correctable. The decisive concerns are instead the missing matched-codec/end-to-end efficiency evidence and the limited, insufficiently controlled empirical validation of the main contributions. The idea is promising, but the current evidence favors weak rejection.

strengths: The paper explores an original and relevant direction: treating 2D Gaussian splats as the native input representation for vision-language alignment rather than merely compressing patch tokens after encoding.

The work has substantial engineering scope. Batched 2DGS fitting, structured initialization, offline conversion of 12.8M DataComp images, and adaptation of a pretrained CLIP backbone together constitute a meaningful systems-and-modeling contribution.

The splat-aware stem and two-stage RGB-to-GS distillation procedure are technically plausible and supported by useful ablations over stem architectures, normalization, distillation objectives, training strategies, point budgets, and token counts.

Evaluation spans many heterogeneous zero-shot classification datasets and reports per-dataset results rather than only aggregates. The paper also candidly identifies important limitations, including expensive fitting, poor training from scratch, sensitivity to distribution shift, and dependence on an RGB teacher.

Structured initialization shows a clear reconstruction advantage over random initialization, while the results demonstrate that aggressively reduced Gaussian representations can retain considerable semantic information.
weaknesses: The central transmission-efficiency claim is not adequately supported. Compression is measured against uncompressed 8-bit RGB, not JPEG or modern image codecs actually used for edge-cloud transmission. For example, 3136 splats require about 50 KB in FP16, which may not outperform an ordinary compressed 224x224 image. No rate-accuracy comparison against codecs, compressed-domain models, transmission energy, or end-to-end communication latency is provided.

The efficiency evaluation excludes important costs. Reported speedups cover data loading and decoding, but not the Perceiver stem, whose cross-attention processes up to 3136 splats, nor full encoder latency, FLOPs, memory, or the substantial offline fitting cost. Consequently, reducing the backbone to 98 latent tokens does not by itself establish lower end-to-end computation.

The headline claim of retaining 96-98% of baseline accuracy relies on averaging dataset-wise accuracy ratios. In absolute terms, the best GS result is 20.39 versus 22.20 for RGB, or about 91.8%. Ratio averaging is unstable on datasets where the baseline is near chance and obscures severe failures, such as diabetic-retinopathy accuracy falling from 38.33 to roughly 3-8. Results also lack multiple seeds or uncertainty estimates.

The strongest adapted 98-token RGB baseline in the appendix reaches 20.56 mean accuracy, exceeding every 98-token GS model, but the main comparison emphasizes an unfine-tuned token-merging baseline at 18.52. Training and compute matching between RGB and GS models is therefore insufficiently controlled.

The systems evidence contains ambiguities and inconsistencies. Appendix Table 3 labels the increase in total batch fitting time relative to batch size one as 'Speedup'; its kernel/memory percentages describe fractions of active GPU time rather than demonstrating the claimed 97% overall utilization. The reported greater-than-90x improvement lacks sufficiently detailed, matched absolute measurements and numerical-equivalence checks against the prior implementation.

The pruning contribution is largely disconnected from the main vision-language results, which use non-pruned FP16 splats. It is evaluated on only 100 Mini-ImageNet images using PSNR, without downstream accuracy. Moreover, pruning by color luminance ignores Gaussian support and can remove semantically important dark structures; the illustrated 23.72% pruning already reduces PSNR from 37.43 to 31.1 dB.

The study is limited to one relatively weak, reduced-width CLIP model and one pretraining dataset, with zero-shot classification as the only downstream task. It does not evaluate retrieval or an actual VLM despite motivating the method through multimodal reasoning and token-context constraints.

Reproducibility is incomplete because code and CUDA kernels are only promised for future release, measurement methodology is underspecified, and some reporting is inconsistent: the manuscript repeatedly states 38 benchmarks, while the detailed result table appears to contain 37 datasets. Overall, the novel representation study is promising, but the evidence does not yet decisively validate its principal end-to-end efficiency narrative.

strengths: The paper explores a timely and potentially useful direction: using 2D Gaussian splats as the direct input representation for vision-language encoders rather than merely as a rendering primitive.
The study is unusually large for an alternative image representation, preprocessing 12.8M DataComp samples and evaluating zero-shot classification across 38 datasets and four Gaussian budgets.

The two-stage RGB-to-GS distillation and parameter-efficient CLIP adaptation are technically sensible. The appendix includes useful architecture, normalization, distillation, and scratch-training studies.
The batched fitting implementation, structured initialization, and extensive throughput profiling could constitute a valuable systems contribution if released and evaluated more rigorously.
weaknesses: The central edge-cloud efficiency claim is not adequately supported. Compression is measured only against uncompressed 8-bit RGB, without comparisons to JPEG/WebP/AVIF, learned codecs, or other compact machine-oriented representations at matched accuracy or bitrate. A 23.5x reduction from raw RGB is not sufficient evidence of transmission superiority in realistic systems.

There is no end-to-end compute, latency, memory, or energy evaluation. Producing each representation requires 2,000 optimization iterations and GPU preprocessing, while the Perceiver must attend over as many as 3,136 splats before producing 98 or 196 tokens. Reporting only local data-loading/decoding time omits these major costs and does not establish the claimed computational or edge-deployment benefits.

Some systems reporting is technically confusing or incorrect. In Table 3, the reported 'Speedup' is simply the increase in batch wall time relative to batch size 1 (e.g., 327/7 = 46.71), whereas the throughput speedup for batch size 4,096 would be about 87.7x. Moreover, the reported kernel/memory fractions of active GPU time are not equivalent to the claimed 97% GPU utilization. These issues weaken confidence in the headline 90x systems result.

The claimed accuracy retention obscures consequential failures. Although GS-3136 obtains 0.98 mean relative accuracy, its absolute average is 20.39 versus 22.20 for RGB, and it collapses on diabetic retinopathy from 38.33% to 3.09% and FER-2013 from 17.41% to 7.19%. Averaging dataset-wise ratios, especially over tasks with near-chance baseline accuracy, can make the representation appear more competitive than the absolute results warrant. The paper provides no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or significance analysis.

The pruning contribution is disconnected from the main vision-language experiments, which explicitly use non-pruned FP16 splats. Its evidence is limited to 100 Mini-ImageNet images, and the highlighted setting removes only 23.72% of points while losing 6.33 dB PSNR. Treating low luminance as low information is also questionable because dark text, boundaries, and objects can be semantically important.

The evaluation does not isolate whether 2DGS is preferable to ordinary lossy reconstruction. The rendered-RGB control is shown only as an ImageNet training curve, rather than a full matched comparison across the 38 benchmarks and compression levels. Consequently, the results may primarily demonstrate distillation from an RGB teacher under lossy preprocessing, not a distinctive advantage of Gaussian representations.

Reproducibility is incomplete: the code and custom CUDA kernels are only promised after publication, and important fitting and timing details are insufficient to independently verify the preprocessing and throughput claims. Several ablations report only early one-epoch ImageNet accuracy rather than final multi-dataset results.

Overall, the representation and scale are worthwhile, but the unsupported comparison to realistic compression pipelines, omission of end-to-end costs, inconsistencies in systems metrics, and substantial uncharacterized accuracy failures are material weaknesses rather than presentation refinements. The current evidence therefore favors rejection.

strengths: The paper presents an original and potentially useful direction: treating 2D Gaussian splats as the native input to a vision-language encoder rather than merely as a rendering or reconstruction representation.

The systems contribution is substantial. Batched CUDA execution, structured initialization, and large-scale preprocessing make it possible to fit all 12.8M DataComp images; the reported profiling shows up to 90.3× speedup over the referenced implementation and provides fitting times across batch sizes.

The two-stage adaptation is technically sensible and parameter-efficient: RGB-to-GS feature distillation followed by limited CLIP adaptation reuses a pretrained transformer while training only about 9.7–13.8% of the full model parameters.

The evaluation is broad across natural, fine-grained, OCR, medical, and synthetic classification datasets. GS-3136 and GS-1600 retain average relative accuracies of 0.98 and 0.96, respectively, while reducing the uncompressed input representation by approximately 3× and 5.9×; even GS-400 retains about 0.91 relative accuracy at 23.5× reduction.

The appendix contains useful architectural and optimization studies, including distillation strategies and losses, normalization, Perceiver versus alternative stems, point transformers, training from scratch, token counts, and rendered-GS controls. The manuscript also candidly identifies dependence on an RGB teacher and weaker robustness under distribution shift.
weaknesses: The headline edge-cloud efficiency claim is not established end to end. Compression ratios use raw 8-bit RGB as the denominator and FP16 splats as the alternative, without comparison to JPEG, WebP, AVIF, learned codecs, or the quantized Gaussian representation discussed in related work. Likewise, the reported speedup measures local data loading and decoding, not network transmission, energy, or latency.

Producing the representation remains expensive: every image is optimized for 2,000 iterations on H100 GPUs, requiring 25.6–53.1 GPU-hours per 12.8M-point-budget dataset configuration. No evidence shows that this fitting can run efficiently on the resource-constrained edge devices motivating the paper. Thus, the method is currently most convincing as an offline representation study rather than a deployable edge-cloud pipeline.

The pruning contribution is disconnected from the principal vision-language results: CLIP experiments use fixed, non-pruned FP16 splats, while pruning is evaluated only through reconstruction PSNR on 100 Mini-ImageNet images. Moreover, the displayed example loses 6.33 dB after pruning only 23.72% of splats, and luminance thresholding may remove semantically meaningful dark content. Downstream accuracy after pruning is needed to support semantic-preservation claims.

Comparison fairness is imperfect. The GS models inherit and distill from the fully trained RGB baseline and then receive additional contrastive adaptation, so the reported parameter-efficient training excludes the cost of producing the RGB teacher. The 98-token RGB comparison based on pairwise token averaging is weak, although the appendix's five-epoch adaptation partially addresses this concern.

Results are reported as single values without multiple seeds, variance, or significance analysis. This limits confidence in small differences among GS configurations and in claims that GS outperforms RGB on individual datasets. Some ablations are presented only as small plots rather than exact numerical results.

The manuscript repeatedly states evaluation on 38 datasets, but Tables 5 and 6 appear to contain 37 dataset rows. Reproducibility is also weakened by reliance on a promise of future code release and incomplete reporting of fitting optimizer settings, evaluation prompts, random seeds, augmentation, and full training cost. These are correctable reporting issues rather than fundamental defects.
